newsitem.title: UK: UK boundary changes make Labour task a bit harder.
newsitem.headline: UK boundary changes make Labour task a bit harder.

text.p: Changes to constituency boundaries will make it slightly harder for Britain's main opposition Labour party to win an overall parliamentary majority at the next general election, according to political analysts.

The constituency map of Britain has been changed four times in the past 50 years to reflect population shifts -- principally a move out of the cities and into the suburbs -- but the latest review will be have a much milder impact than the previous set of changes implemented in 1983.

Nevertheless, a definitive study of the revisions by political scientists Colin Rallings and Michael Thrasher said the ruling Conservatives would have had an overall majority of 27 instead of 21 if they had been in place at the 1992 election.
The changes, which increase the number of members of parliament to 659 from 651, also mean Labour will need a bigger swing in the vote to oust John Major's Conservatives from power.
In 1992, the Conservatives would have lost their overall majority on a swing to Labour of just 0.5 percent. Under the redrawn boundaries, the figure would have been 0.8 percent.
Similarly, the swing needed by Labour to secure an overall majority rises under the changes to 4.3 from 4.1 percent.

Either would be a record, exceeding the 3.2 percent swing Labour enjoyed in its favour at the 1964 election, but Rallings and Thrasher commented: "A stiff task certainly, but more a matter of degree than of substance."

"Any uniform swing from Conservative to Labour of greater than 0.8 percent and less than 4.3 percent at the next general election will produce a hung Parliament, with no one party having an overall majority."

Labour would need a bigger swing, partly because of the way new marginal seats are distributed. Also, the Conservatives find themselves in second place in a higher proportion of Labour marginal seats than Labour is in Conservative constituenices.
"The cumulative effect is to make it more difficult for Labour to secure a comfortable overall majority than under the old boundaries," the two analysts said.
Nevertheless, the review by the four independent Boundary Commissions -- for England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland -- could have been a lot worse for Labour.
Some commentators had predicted prior to the review that the Conservatives could benefit by as many as 20 seats, not six.
"On the whole... Labour has emerged from the review of constituency boundaries in a less disadvantaged position than it must have feared," Rallings and Thrasher commented.

In particular, the boundary changes fail to remove a bias in the electoral system that favours Labour because of the concentration of its vote in smaller seats. Conservative constituencies, by contrast, tend to be larger.
As a result Labour will continue to get more seats than the Conservatives for any given share of the vote.
If both parties polled 39 percent of the vote in 1992, Labour would have won 38 more seats than the Conservatives. Under revised boundaries, the lead is cut, but only to 33 seats.
This means that Labour might be able to secure an overall majority with a slender one percent lead in the popular vote, Rallings and Thrasher said.

The Conservatives, however, will require a lead in the popular vote of 4-8 percentage points to retain a bare majority. In 1992, they had a lead of 7.5 percentage points, outpolling Labour 41.9 percent to 34.4 percent.

"These figures may even understate the problem. Ever since the Boundary Commissions began their work (in 1991, 1992 and 1993), continuing shifts in population will have led to a further increase in the averge electorate size of Conservative constituencies and a decrease in Labour ones," they said.
